9.title: One of the greatest comebacks in Hollywood history
9.content:
The first time I watched "Batman Begins", I only gave it a 5 or a 6, I couldn't remember. Watching it for the second time, I knew where I went wrong the first time I rated it.

It's only because I compared it to the other four movies of the Batman franchise. But "Batman Begins" is so different from the other films that it cannot be classed as part from this franchise. Director Christopher Nolan has literally created the Batman Franchise 2.

And like Tim Burton did in the first series of movies, Nolan brings an explosive, surprising and visually-dazzling adventure which gives hope to those who thought that Batman's movie career died because of Joel Schumacher's ill-fated vision.

Burton's Gothic landscape of Gotham City is dead too, but some characteristics remain. Essentially the dark and sinister atmosphere that flows on the town. Instead, Gotham City looks like a modern metropolis and we can feel that the action happens nowadays. I can interpret this as a mean for getting closer to the spectator, which is welcomed.

In a global way, every aspect of the movie is designed in order to give a more realistic look to Batman. Not only visually, but psychologically and socially. And especially psychologically.

The introduction shows a Bruce Wayne (Christian Bale) full of rage and despair after his parents were murdered in front of his eyes. This event deeply traumatized him and his desire of vengeance brings him to the Far East. There, he meets mysterious Henri Ducard (Liam Neeson), who is a member of the powerful and secret organization known as the League of Shadows, which operates for global justice in very unique and arguable ways.

Ducard teaches Wayne how to fight his enemies and how to canalize his rage and his fears. The young billionaire returns to his manor and, with the help of his butler Alfred (Michael Caine) and Lucius Fox (Morgan Freeman), a scientist working for Wayne Enterprises, Wayne becomes the hero that we all know: the Caped Crusader himself.

Christopher Nolan sounded like a risky choice for the role of director. "Memento" and "Insomnia" were impressive psychological thrillers, but a superhero film (especially from a shattered franchise) is not the same ballpark. But surprisingly, Nolan doesn't change his techniques and that's what helps the movie working.

Nolan gives a lot of attention to the psychology of his characters (something that Burton and Schumacher did in a minimalist way) and his unique special effects are dazzling, exciting and adequately nightmarish.

Some scenes are catchier than others. But I think that the movie's trademark is the horror images coming from the toxin that plays a major role in the story. The shimmering effect created by the camera and the horrific images and voice of The Scarecrow (Cillian Murphy) are easily the best FX ever made in a Batman movie.

And let's not forget the bat invasion near the end of the movie, which could be dubbed as Christopher Nolan's "The Bats", creating a parallel with Alfred Hitchcock's "The Birds".

The story is first-rate and the action scenes are worthy of the best Bruckheimer movies. But mixed together so well is almost a miraculous move.

"Batman Begins" shows actors at the top of their shapes. Christian Bale is a superb Batman, probably the best of all. Liam Neeson is a scary villain, proving that he's not only able of portraying heroic good guys (Oskar Schindler and Qui-Gon Jinn). Katie Holmes owns her name instead of Mrs. Cruise's one and Gary Oldman gets the role of his life as scrupulously honest police officer Gordon.

The only false note that I would give to this movie is that it ends way too quickly and brings its conclusion too fast. The story can get very complex (even if it's also a plus) and some of the characters' philosophical and moral speeches can distract from the real story.

Do you believe in miracles? Because this movie is one of them. Batman lives again with this terrific redemption film and there's definitely a dove in the sky, which might be accompanied by a bat.

9.title: "It's not who I am underneath, but what I do that defines me."
9.content:
FILM: 8.5/10.

Eight years after the Batman franchise was driven into the ground by Joel Schumacher at the direction of Warner Bros and their need for a merchandising and kid-friendly film, an unlikely person steps up to the plate: Christopher Nolan. I really enjoyed his earlier works, so when I heard he was taking the reigns of a character I love, I was intrigued.

Nolan delivers a largely realistic take on the Dark Knight, focusing more on the psychology of Batman, and it's great. The gritty atmosphere of Gotham City is palpable, and the exploration of Bruce Wayne's inner demons adds depth to the character. Christian Bale was an interesting choice following his turn as Patrick Bateman in American Psycho, and he is imposing in the role. He captures both the darkness and the vulnerability of Batman, making him a truly believable hero.

Nolan's decision to cast quite a few heavyweights around him in the form of Michael Caine, Morgan Freeman, and Gary Oldman means there's a depth of quality too. Caine brings warmth and wisdom as Alfred, Freeman is the perfect fit as the brilliant Lucius Fox, and Oldman shines as the determined and incorruptible Commissioner Gordon. The chemistry among the cast members elevates the film and adds another layer of enjoyment.

We still get the gadgets and there's more than enough action to satisfy any fan of the Caped Crusader. However, it's interesting to note that the action becomes more generic once the technological MacGuffin is introduced. The film shines brightest in its exploration of Batman's origins and his transformation into the symbol of justice Gotham needs.

Batman Begins is an impressive injection of life into a franchise killed by Bat-nipples, neon, and terrible jokes. Nolan's direction and the darker tone bring a refreshing and mature approach to the character. The film successfully sets the stage for a new era of Batman on the big screen, leaving me eager for more. It also had a tantalizing stinger at the end that hints at exciting possibilities for future installments.

Batman Begins is a must-watch for any Batman fan. Nolan's vision and the exceptional performances by the cast make it a standout entry in the superhero genre. It revitalizes the character and sets the foundation for the remarkable trilogy to follow.

9.title: The story behind the Caped Crusader's mask
9.content:
We all know what happened to the original Batman franchise; what started out as a rather promising trilogy ended as being nothing more than a campy final two movies.

Christopher Nolan, one of the best directors of the 21st Century, has risen to the challenge of creating a new Batman franchise. His first task? Reveal the true story of Batman's mysterious past and deliver it in the most magnificent way possible.

The movie begins with Bruce Wayne in a place in life you've never seen before. He is in a prison in Nepal (?), for committing crime. He is soon approached by a man named Henri Ducard, a man who is looking to give Bruce Wayne a chance to clean up the hell he has put himself in and turn him into a man of justice. Bruce Wayne, who has hit rock bottom, has decided to start making his way back upward and fulfill his goals and needs. This is the opening story of the movie.

The first thirty minutes transcends between Bruce's time with the League of Shadows (a comic book origin not even hinted at in previous Batman films) and the path he has taken in life, leading up to where he is right now. Through these recollections, we discover why Bruce Wayne is terrified of bats, his drives, wishes, and most importantly we get a 3-dimensional look at the type of person he is.

The next thirty minutes is fast-paced, showing his return to Gotham city. Although corrupt, The League of Shadows has taught him how to fight injustice. He quickly acquires a disguise, a symbol, and his first mission is to put Carmine Falcone behind bars. This is where Batman finally comes in. He thwarts a drug shipment, and Falcone is finally handcuffed, waiting for his trial.

What Batman doesn't realize is that this move has played right into the hands of insane asylum-owner Dr. Jonathan Crane, played to perfection by the creepy Cillian Murphy. He takes over the empire Falcone once owned and seemingly has his own plans. Soon, a microwave transmitter is stolen, and Batman slowly begins to unravel the connection between Jonathan Crane (aka "The Scarecrow"), the shipment of drugs, and the stolen microwave transmitter.

The plot planned by the Scarecrow and Ra's Al Ghul is easily the most sinister of any Batman film, driven by motivations that were missing from previous Caped Crusader films.

That's not the only thing about this Batman film that I liked better than other interpretations of Batman's story lines. Bruce Wayne's history is outlined and detailed with a brilliant passion, and only enhanced by Christian Bale's performance. His character has excellent chemistry with Henri Ducard, who is played by the outstanding Liam Neeson. His bout with Batman at the end is exhilarating, and it makes the best fight scene in any Batman film. His confrontations with the Scarecrow are even better- although there are only two, his first is the most memorable, being one of the coolest scenes I have ever seen(not greatest, COOLEST). Cillian Murphy never shows any vulnerability as The Scarecrow, although he is ultimately "defeated" (or is he?).

Not to say BB was perfect. I didn't like some of the little things (like a homeless man approaching the Batmobile and saying "Nice ride"), some of the scenes didn't seem to enhance the film (Do I look like a cop?), and the love story was a one-way road. While Christian Bale actually showed that he liked Rachel Dawes (Katie Holmes), Katie Holmes didn't seem to react, making the love story seem a bit off when all of a sudden Rachel Dawes kisses him at the end of the movie. However, Katie Holmes was a great DA and the chemistry between her and Cillian Murhpy in there scenes together worked like a charm.

So even though Batman Begins is not without its flaws, it more than manages to entertain the average moviegoer, answers the questions of a lot of people as to Bruce Wayne, offers a little something for everyone, and leaves the viewer satisfied. 9.5/10= Amazing movie!

9.title: Batman Reborn
9.content:
It seems odd that a character who has been brought to the screen so many times in so many different manners as Batman has never had a proper "origin story" until now. True, several earlier film versions sketched in the basics--little Bruce Wayne witnesses his parents' murder, inspiring a one-man crusade against evil--but none of them struck at the heart of the matter, namely: how and why exactly does a wealthy child of privilege decide to not only devote his life fighting crime, but to do so dressed as a flying rodent? Christopher Nolan's "Batman Begins" answers that question along with a few others, but even more remarkably, it renews a franchise that had been driven into the ground by its own excesses.

And make no mistake, it is a rebirth, not a continuation--Nolan wisely rebuilds Batman from the ground up, rather than pick up where others had left off. This is a Gotham City far removed from the Gothic grandeur of Tim Burton's vision, and even farther removed from the gaudy camp of Joel Schumacher's. Nolan's Gotham is a sprawling urban nightmare of a city, with cold industrial towers looming against the sky while beneath the poor struggle for survival in the Narrows, a decaying skid row where even the police fear to tread. Most of the city officials are in the pockets of crime lords or are in fear of them. The few who aren't, such as honest cop Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman, radiating weary nobility) and idealistic young attorney Rachael Dawes (Katie Hudson) lack the clout to fight back. With such an example, it's easy to see why Bruce Wayne (Christian Bale) would become disillusioned with society's normal method of justice, and embark on a personal quest to understand and combat crime.

The early part of "Batman Begins" establishes this background, intercut with Bruce's training with the ancient and mysterious League of Shadows. His mentor (Liam Neeson) describes the society as being devoted to restoring justice, but Bruce soon comes to disagree with their methods. The League thinks society is past repair and wants to eradicate it; Bruce would rather help those trying to fix the problem. Perhaps if he acted as a source of inspiration, a figurehead in the battle against evil

"Batman Begins" follows the recent trend in comic-book films, creating a story that is as much driven by charactersspecifically the central characteras it is by action. Bale is an ideal choice for the title role: handsome enough to be convincing as a millionaire playboy, and talented enough to convey the shadows in Bruce Wayne's soul. He also does something with Batman that has been seen all too infrequently: he makes him genuinely frightening. With the possible exception of Michael Keaton, no Batman has ever credibly established himself as someone who could strike terror in the heart of even the most hardened and cynical criminal. Bale, speaking in a harsh growl and moving with almost inhuman speed and silence, is naturally intimidatingno wonder both the police and the thugs hesitate to confront him. Nolan has surrounded Bale with brilliant supporting playersin addition to Oldman and Neeson, we have Michael Caine exuding quiet loyalty and dry British wit as faithful butler Alfred, and Morgan Freeman making the most of the scientist who supplies the fledgling Batman with most of his toys. The bad guys' side is rounded out by Tom Wilkinson as Gotham's reigning crime boss, and Cillian Murphy as twisted psychiatrist Dr. Crane. Crane, whose disturbingly serene manner carries echoes of Norman Bates, experiments on his patients with a panic-inducing drug that proves central in tying the various story lines together. In the thankless role of the love interest, Hudson adds a personal dimension to Bruce's crusade but never induces much romantic tensionwe know Wayne's bachelor status is never in any real jeopardy. But if that's as bad as it gets, then "Batman Begins" is very good indeed. Would that all major "event" movies turned out so well.

9.title: Better in Every Aspect
9.content:
"Batman Begins" is a story that is completely separate from the first four Batman movies--which, toward it's latest installments, nosedived into the abyss of Hollywood big budget folly. It not only provides the origin of Bruce Wayne's transformation into the legend of Batman, and it does so with such guarded care and attention that one can easily appreciate upon viewing.

But it is more than just a separate movie franchise, but an improved one in every aspect of film-making. Actors are better--Christian Bale is wonderful as both a billionaire "Prince of Gotham" and a crime fighter that strikes fear in the hearts of many. Throw in Michael Caine's rendition, a great performance, as Alfred and--oh why not--Morgan Freeman as a man akin to "Q" in the 007 franchise, and you've got quite an ensemble of polished performers.

It isn't just the acting itself that is a great improvement, but the construct of the characters themselves. Bruce Wayne, as it turns out, is a lot more complicated and vulnerable man than any of the other screen renditions would suggest. I've read some reviewers say that the movie lacks a great villain, perhaps longing for Jack Nicholson's "Joker", but I disagree. The villains in "Batman Begins" are not reduced to simple maniacal monsters nor cartoonish fools (nor Arnold Schwarzenegger--yikes!). Their motivations may be irrational and downright sociopathic, but one is at least presented with a reason for their criminal intent.

And perhaps that is the best part of this version of Batman films: the superb direction by Christopher Nolan. Rightly biding his time and making the full use of the 140 minutes of runtime, Nolan paces the "Batman Begins" with a superior understanding of how great cinemas engage the audience. We are not racking our brains just to catch up to the plot--a technique actually often employed by movie makers when they don't want us to realize the holes in the plot--and we're not bored to submission. The progress is just right, and when the action turns on, it drives us full force in a thrilling joyride.

Better acting, better script, better characters and better directing. Minus the absurd silliness of the last couple of Batman flicks, and you've got the best of the bunch, by far. I've always enjoyed Tim Burton's original work, but this is an improvement by leaps and bounds.

But then again, could you really do any worse than "Batman and Robin"?

9.title: Is batman a Nolan archetype?
9.content:
What I enjoyed most in "Batman Begins" was its effort to be realistic: Batman's suit is made of a special material, whose properties are realistically described and portrayed. His car does things we have seen in TV shows and in footage from real car chases: realism is more important than speed in this car and in the film itself.

But don't be fooled: Nolan does not try to convince us that a "batman" could exist thanks to a strong will, intensive training and modern technology. Realism is just the perfect guideline to make a fiction more complex, deeper, and more interesting to analyze (if you want to), with a richer texture and many details that you can pick on second viewing.

This batman does not live in our universe, but at least his universe is almost as complex as our own, and not that oversimplification of the previous batman films. Nolan creates an interesting atmosphere, as he does in his other films, and brings back his usual obsessions on identity, the illusions of mind and the actions that define us.

And after all... in what film do you hear someone talking about "jungian archetypes"? Another touch of realism and a psychological joke, something you could expect from the director of "Memento".

9 out of 10. I can't wait to see "The Dark Knight".

9.title: I like how this "Begins"
9.content:
With the exception of Superman IV: The Quest for Peace, no other comic book film franchise has gone into hibernation with as weak a final entry as the Batman series. 1997's Batman & Robin, filled with camp, bad one-liners, an overstuffed cast and just general corniness seemed to have felled the Caped Crusader semi-permanently. Eight years later, director Christopher Nolan and screenwriter David Goyer have breathed new life into Batman with Batman Begins, the best entry in the Batman series yet and one of the best comic book adaptations to date.

Jettisoning all the baggage of the previous Batman films, Nolan and Goyer have started fresh, electing to focus on Batman's origin. They succeed brilliantly in placing the film's focus on the title character for the first time, and also follow in suit of X-Men by treating the material as seriously as possible.

As Batman Begins opens, Bruce Wayne (Christian Bale), a millionaire heir to his late father's fortune, is traveling the world, attempting to learn as much about the criminal element as possible by acting as a criminal. He is approached by Henri Ducard (Liam Neeson), a lieutenant of Ra's Al Ghul (Ken Watanabe), the leader of the League of Shadows, an organization dedicated to eradicating crime in the world. While training with the League, we are treated to flashbacks of Bruce as a child, living near crime infested Gotham City, discovering a large cave under his family's elaborate mansion, Wayne Manor, and being attacked by bats, which Bruce quickly develops a fear of. Shortly thereafter, Bruce's father and mother are killed in a mugging and Bruce is raised by his faithful butler, Alfred (Michael Caine). Robbed of an opportunity to shoot his parent's killer, and intimidated by the local crime boss, Carmine Falcone (Tom Wilkinson), Bruce begins his trek. Upon completion of his training with the League, he discovers that they are a little more ruthless than he realized and splits with them, returning to his home city of Gotham to fight crime his own way. With the assistance of Lucius Fox (Morgan Freeman),the head of the special research division of his father's company, Wayne Enterprises, Bruce discovers some advanced technology that he fashions into a suit that he wears to combat crime in the guise of his greatest fear, bats. As Bruce unveils his crime-fighting persona, Batman, Gotham City is being threatened by a hallucinogenic drug being imported to the city by psychiatrist Johnathan Crane (Cillian Murphy), also known as the Scarecrow. Assisted by honest Gotham detective James Gordan (Gary Oldman) and his childhood sweetheart, Assistant D.A. Rachel Dawes (Katie Holmes), Batman determines he must unravel the plot the Scarecrow is weaving before it destroys Gotham.

Since the release of the first Batman movie in 1989, one character in the franchise has remained a mystery on the big screen: Bruce Wayne himself. The prior films always focused on the outrageous villains and elaborate production design, relegating Batman to the background. Here, he is center stage. Batman Begins is very much a character study of Bruce Wayne, as learns to take all the fear, hatred and guilt that he has pent up since he saw his parents die and transform himself into a force of justice to combat the crime that is engulfing Gotham City. He struggles with his guilt, leaving everything he knows behind to immerse himself in criminal culture to eventually learn why the criminal ticks. However, despite his desire to see criminals brought to justice, he still maintains a sense of mercy that prevents him from going too far.

Another strong point is the creation of a recognizable reality. Sure, a world where a man dresses in a suit designed to look like a bat is not what I would call realistic, but Batman Begins comes as close as possible. Gotham City is based off of real-world Chicago, and passes for a real, living, breathing city. There are plausible explanations created for Batman's hardware and equipment. Nolan and production designer Nathan Crowley's realistic approach lends a greater weight to the story.

The villains and their plot also have a strong connection to the character development of Bruce Wayne, not just some random goal that sounds as if it was concocted by a screenwriter just so there could be some excuse for the film to exist. While some of the details of the overall scheme are a bit shaky, the overall plot is integral to the film, not just an afterthought. Also, Batman is depicted working at solving a mystery, not just reacting to the events going on around him. He is something of a detective here, unlike before where he seemed to be a bit player.

However, the film has weaknesses. While I enjoyed the focus on the character of Bruce Wayne, the villains are somewhat underutilized, at times seeming almost inconsequential. Unlike Spider-Man 2, where Doctor Octopus was a fully-realized, three-dimensional character on par with Peter Parker, here the villains for the most part service the plot and little else. Cillian Murphy is very effective as the Scarecrow, no doubt, but doesn't quite stake out a claim to fame in the comic villains hall of fame. The character of Rachael Dawes is also a weak link in the chain, proving to be a generic love interest and little else. Katie Holmes does her best, but the chemistry between her and Nolan is nonexistent.

Christian Bale gives the strongest performance yet for the character of Bruce Wayne. He brings intensity and drive to the character, and fills out the various aspects of Bruce Wayne. Instead of just serving as a placeholder, Bale gives Bruce Wayne presence. The rest of the supporting cast, especially Michael Caine and Morgan Freeman, perform admirably, giving Batman Begins a memorable cast overall.

For those who could not believe that a franchise as hobbled as Batman could be rescued, Batman Begins is good evidence that anything can be saved with the right approach.

9.title: The best Batman origin movie
9.content:
Batman Begins is exceptional because it's centered around relatable drama, humanizing the outlandish character. Begins explores Bruce Wayne's radical choices. Instead of leaning on his trauma, the film builds off that, showing growth from vengeance to idealism. Viewers see Gotham's corruption, Wayne's disillusionment, and the reasoning behind his decisions. Supporting characters establish genuine relationships with Wayne. Each one has purpose, perspective, and motivation. Even the villain has twisted logic. Plus, this is all tied together through themes of fear. Collectively, this emotion drives the experience, making the cheesiness forgivable and the developments enthralling.

Meanwhile, the filmmaking is extensive. The visuals aren't artistic, but motion, color, and focus create a grand environment. The editing blends timelines, and the sound is complex yet controlled. Together, they give hallucination sequences an abstract punctuation. The evocative music perfectly matches the tone. The production design is realistic, yet distinctly stunning. Finally, the effects are tangible, utilizing miniatures, stunts, and pyrotechnics for potent action. Overall, Nolan orchestrated an extravagant journey that is grounded in a sentimental mood and an authentic atmosphere. Batman Begins strikes hearts while captivating minds, making it the best Batman origin movie.

Writing: 9/10 Direction: 10/10 Cinematography: 8/10 Acting: 8/10 Editing: 9/10 Sound: 9/10 Score/Soundtrack: 9/10 Production Design: 9/10 Casting: 9/10 Effects: 9/10

Overall Score: 8.9/10.

9.title: Greatest origin story ever?
9.content:
Amazing movie with highly efficient filmmaking. Goes deep into the psychological aspects of Bruce Wayne and how he becomes Batman. Perfect opening to the trilogy. Shows the true essence of Batman. He is a ninja, he uses stealth over brute force.

Phenomenal story and story-telling. A beautiful musical score. Fantastic dialogue, so many quotable lines with deep meaning that continue to stick with you long after viewing. So many goosebump-inducing moments. Masterful directing with the exception of some of the fight scenes. I love this movie so much.

He masters his own childhood fear of bats. Masters, not conquers. He still fears the bats, but lives among them so that he is capable of fully functioning and making proper decisions in the face of fear. He also uses fear against his enemies, "against those who prey on the fearful." The themes are too good.

(7 viewings, 5/7/2024)

9.title: Dark, brooding and unrelentingly realistic take on the Batman mythos
9.content: Dispelling the nightmarish memories of the last two Batman movies, Christopher Nolan reinvents everything and gives us a caped crusader that is as fascinating (and maybe even more so) as the one Burton introduced. Instead of the Gothic atmosphere and black humor of the original, Nolan opts here for unrelenting realism. The first half an hour of the film is so good it defies belief. In fact, it sets the bar for realism so high that the movie falters later on when more comic-like elements are introduced. But the overall result is certainly worth it and a great rendition of the caped crusader's exploits. The film is also blessed with one of the most impressive casts of the decade.

9.title: The BEGINING of one of the best trilogies in history.
9.content:
What can be said about this movie that hasn't already been said... Whoever hasn't seen it yet, I don't know what they're waiting for. I watched the movie when I was a kid, and I still enjoy it with the same excitement as back then.

It has aged really well, considering it's been almost 20 years since its release. If I had to highlight something, it would be the constant action and fun the movie offers. I don't recall a moment where I got bored or stopped paying attention.

It has aged really well, considering it's been almost 20 years since its release. If I had to highlight something, it would be the constant action and fun the movie offers. I don't recall a moment where I got bored or stopped paying attention. Something that surprised me when watching it again was discovering that a young "Prince Joffrey" appears in this movie.

Now stop reading and go watch this amazing movie!!!

9.title: Gritty, realistic and fun - The perfect origin story
9.content:
Having seen the 2 sequels spawned off this film before enjoying it i went in with extremely high expectations as i loved The Dark Knight, i mean who doesn't and despite the overly harsh backlash TDKR has seemed to pick up i was convinced it was the best film ever made when i first watched it... Looking back i may have been wrong but it certainly wasn't "The Godfather 3" of its trilogy and instead was a pleasant send off.

So when i realized i hadn't even seen the first film in this heavily loved franchise i immediately sat down and watched. The film features a terrific ensemble of actors, Bale is great as Bruce Wayne but his Batman is often unintentionally funny when he opens his mouth, Bale puts on an overly gruff and "manly" voice instead of opting for the obvious and copying Kevin Conroy and although this is off-putting it works well in the basis of this story as Wayne is a lost man and it seems as he merely puts on the voice in the heat of the moment and stuck with it.

Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine, Cillian Murphy and Liam Neeson all excel in their roles, and although "Murphy's" demise is underwhelming it is true to the character roots, his character "Scarecrow" a men obsessed with fear and manipulating others with his toxin and mask is often used as leverage for other villains and usually ends up embarrassed and crippled with his own fear and the film doesn't divert far from this notion

Nolan did a great job setting up an often misguided franchise and helped set up an incredible world, Gotham looks stunning and all the characters are believable yet fun... And the film has hardly any flaws and the best part of the whole film is Gary Oldman who plays Commissioner Gordon, in a role he was born for.

9.title: A great revival after Joel Schumacher's trite Batman & Robin
9.content:
I regretted not seeing this in theaters a few years back, but at least I watched it on my DVD copy and boy did I like it. I would hope to re-watch this and The Dark Knight someday if I have the chance.

It tells the story about Bruce Wayne who finds himself in Asia captured in prison and has been brought upon Henri Duncard and Ra's Al Ghoul. They offered him to be trained as a ninja to be given the strength and his chance to change the world, but when Bruce finds out about their plan to destroy Gotham City, the place where he had once been forgotten, things started to change. So, after returning to Gotham City before he reunites with his butler Alfred Pennyworth and his childhood friend Rachel Dawes, crimes started to spread all over Gotham and Bruce transforms himself into a dark superhero. Thus, Batman is born.

After Batman & Robin killed the franchise, it's great to see it being brought back to life with a much darker film like this one. The only problem that I do have with this movie is that it's pretty much overlong, but that doesn't matter. Everything else turned out great.

The acting, aside from some of the greatest visuals I've seen in a comic book movie adaptation, give this movie a great boost of intelligence. Christian Bale gives out one of his best comic book performances as the lead character and was just as we imagined him to be: dark, brooding, and charismatic. Katie Holmes was beautiful as Rachel Dawes as is Michael Caine, Morgan Freeman, and Gary Oldman. Liam Neeson and Ken Watanabe did great as the villains in this movie.

The music from Hans Zimmer is nicely composed and although, not the best music he's ever composed, is still worth-listening to. It also has some great cinematography and some solid editing, but the action sequences and the story are the greatest aspects of the entire movie. The plot had some heart-wrenching moments including the death of Bruce's parents and some great interactions between Bruce and other characters and the action sequences are some of the best I've seen with Batman fighting against Ra's Al Ghoul and the others and the climax between Batman and Henri as my favorites.

Overall, Batman Begins is not the best superhero movie I've ever seen, but this is still a great reboot that pays it's respects to the Batman character and I've seen much worse movies at my time. It's worth-watching for die-hard fans of the Batman comics and franchise.

9.title: Batman begins properly
9.content:
Ever since the Batman series took a wrong turn somewhere in the 90's, I was a little sceptic when I heard there was going to be a new one. This quickly turned to curiosity upon hearing Nolan was to direct it.

And once again, he hit the right spot with this movie. Instead of introducing a colourful batman and his adversaries, he gave us the blessing of not even seeing batman in the first hour of the movie! The entire film is built up fantastically around how Batman came to be, why he did and how. The movie isn't even about how he fights the bad guy:it's about how he himself develops. Thus, we get lots of fine dialoguecombined with a healthy amount of action as Batman tries to save Gotham.

This movie is an excellent reboot of the series, and sets a standard for superheroe movies in the future.

9.title: A Perfect Re-Imagining!
9.content: This was basically DC Comics' last attempt at redeeming their dying batman movie franchise, and it was hook line and sinker! Not only the best BATMAN movie to date, but by far the best super-hero movie outside of the SPIDERMAN franchise. Christopher Nolan crafted a masterpiece of an origin film, completely re-imagining the telling of the mysterious BRUCE WAYNE and his alter-ego, BATMAN. The fact that BATMAN wasn't even on screen into half way through this 2 1/2 hour long film doesn't even seem to phase you through the expert story telling of how Bruce Wayne flees Gotham City to learn to fight her crime. The villains of the movie may be new to the non-fan base audience but us batman fans loved cillian murphy as professor jonathan crane. a perfect reincarnation of the comic book character that he represented, the only thing that he did wrong was not appear in the film enough. really, the central villain of the film comes out of nowhere. the movie is more about the humanistic elements of bruce wayne and batman than about villains. not to mention, nolan relied on the actors as opposed to some other super-hero movies that exist solely to show of what a computer can do. bottom line, stop everything you are doing and go see this movie now!

9.title: One of the better Batman movies; Highly Recommend
9.content:
Overall: This movie was dark, gritty and in general a nice, fresh take on the Batman character. There is a reason people saved Batman, this is part of it.

Good: Phenomenal acting from Heroes and Villains alike. Bale, Caine, Freeman and Oldman provide great performances, not career highlights by any means but great nonetheless. Despite this,in typical Nolan fashion, the villains stand out from the rubble and I must say Liam Neeson did a great job as Ra's Al Ghul(and they pronounced it correctly!). Cillian Murphy provides a creepy, unsettling Scarecrow which should be as standard for the character. Great story with excellent dialogue. Impeccable cinematography and music. Outstanding effects, once more it is a Nolan movie.

Bad: The cops are 100% morons(which sadly doesn't change). This would be acceptable in an Adam West Batman or Joel Schumacher but for the gritty, REALISTIC interpretation it is simply unacceptable. A minor annoyance, but rapid swapping from past and present can be a tad bit annoying but it is a Nolan movie. Another more minor complaint, but as it is an origin story, their is much less action scenes and set pieces as the other movies. The action was good when it happened but was too infrequent for that to matter.

Best Part: The training montage between Bruce and 'Henry Ducard'.

MVP: Liam Neeson as Ra's Al Ghul

9/10

9.title: Substance over style
9.content:
Though I'm not an avid graphic novel reader, I do like the medium because it plays out like a movie, and the plots are more complex than are put on screen. However, many movies which try to adapt graphic novels to screen mutilate the original in the process (with the exception of the recent "Sin City").

"Batman Begins", however, is not based on any graphic novel. But by the way it was written and directed, it sure could have been. This has to be the most mature Batman to hit the screen. Gone is the campiness of the original series, and the hallucinogenic visions of the last 4 Batman films. This Batman/Bruce Wayne, while younger, probably has more innovation in a single frame than the previous Batman films. There is more insight on what he does to take out his frustrations, and how he channels them. We also see how he is capable of making a Batcave, how he makes the gadgets that he uses, and finally, how human Batman really is (as witnessed by the number of bruises he gets after a night of fighting.

Christian Bale has always been a pretty decent actor, and as Bruce Wayne/Batman, he brings more depth into the role and any of the 4 actors who played him previously. Liam Neeson was a surprise as Ducard, and handles the role well. Likewise for Cillian Murphy, Gary Oldman, Michael Caine, and Rutger Hauer. As for Katie Holmes, she's adequate.

If I had one gripe about the film, it was that the some of the action scenes were choppy and couldn't be appreciated as well as, say, the first Batman. But this point actually makes the case: if you got a gripping story, you don't need cheap theatrics to make it great. Substance over style. Just like an well written graphic novel.

9.title: The best of the Batman franchise
9.content:
I think this is the best Batman movie to the date yet, it was great but at the same time risky the idea of reinvent the franchise because 4 movies were made after this with success except the fourth one that didn't surpass the expectactions.

BATMAN BEGINS tells how it really began, starts in the very beginning of Bruce Wayne (played by Christian Bale, the best Batman in my POV) and shows how his parents' deaths changes his life and his fears of the ferocious bats. With the time he even changes more that all his close friends gives him the back and Gothan City becomes an corrupt city without no justice, so he decides to disappear and is stuck on a prison, so he is released by Henri Ducard (Liam Neesom), a recruit of Ra's Al Ghul with the condition for receive the necessary training for fight against crime, but he does not becomes Batman until he comes back to Gotham City and sees how changed the city since he left it and that makes him decides to become something for the population of the city claiming for justice over the corruption that is plagued now. Then he enters the cave that has the ferocious bats that attacked him when he was only a child and now he calls them for fight his fears and become finally in Batman, the man that the thieves -or bad people, whatever how we call it-.

I gives this 9 stars out of 10 stars.

9.title: The Dark Knight Certainly Ain't Dark Shight.....
9.content:
This movie surprised the hell out of me.

I know Christopher Nolan makes good films, so I'm not saying I doubted his abilities. I just thought he did a sterling job of re-vamping a tired series.

Batman and Robin didn't exist, okay. Let's get that into our heads. Arnold Schwarzenegger has never been in a Batman film, m'kay. So going from ice-skates popping out of bat-boots to Batman only really carrying metal shurikens was a great move, because making your protagonist nigh-on invincible makes no one give a damn about them. This exposed weaknesses on Bruce Wayne/Batman's character that can only bring the audience closer to him, and make the film appear grittier and more realistic.

All in all, this is a top-notch film. Very enjoyable, with a wonderful cast of fine actors working with a very good, Gothic director.

9.title: batman as its never been before - since frank miller anyway!!
9.content:
YIPEE!!!! This is the first Batman movie in a while which can be taken seriously, and boy does it feel good to see Gotham City as a dark, crime filled "New York on steroids", as described by Christopher Nolan. This new vision of the batman world is something that continues throughout the film, including the cast.

Bale makes a superb batman, and keeping with the theme of darkness, portrays both Bruce Wayne and his alter ego as a man on the edge. Yet there always seems to be a cold calmness behind his rage.

The rest of the cast is also stand out: Neeson is a very convincing mentor to Wayne, Michael Cane's Alfred delivers some of the best lines in the movie, while Tom Wilkinson and Cillian Murphy make excellent villains, with the latter providing a raging insanity behind cold eyes. And, as always, Morgan Freeman is in a league of his own.

The notion of going back to Batman's roots proves very successful, providing enough back-story to make Wayne's transformation all the more believable. It also makes the donning of the cape and cowl a very special moment.

One minor gripe is Katie Holmes' very unconvincing lawyer. Sadly, she seems to be part of a different film altogether. Thankfully, her appearances are kept to a minimum, so this should in no way put you off.

All in all, a brilliant film, and judging by the ending, we are hopefully in for another Nolan batman outing very soon.

9.title: Incredible movie, though almost batman
9.content:
The movie is incredible for a superhero movie. It's the "wake up" call to Marvel, on how good a well done movie can be with a guy in a leotard.

Probably the best batman yet, Christian Bale is intense, serious, has the voice and even look for the role. The Idea of the Batman costume was to drive fear into criminals - this is from the books not the movie - and it was nice to see that point stressed.

This movie involved more of Bruce Wayne's business than movies before it. There's the squabbles for the company, Bruce's takeover, the introduction of Lucius Fox etc.

Bats aren't overly stressed in this movie. Usually you see grapples in the shape of a bat, the car has bat like fins, Bat this, bat that. The car was well, awesome looking :) and didn't have a thing to do with bats - reminded me of Frank Miller's tank in Dark Knight Returns.

Some things are a little off, some just plain wrong for batman though. Still, a terrific movie for hardcore Batman followers.

Starting with his parents death, the comics always showed his eyes intense, not anger, but close. Definitely not fear.

He did seek to better his body and mind, but it was not running among thieves; and being trained by Ras (pronounced Ray-shh) was a big twist. OK - some things can obviously slide, and the plot fit, but Batman is supposed to have MANY teachers. And Ras isn't supposed to be one of them. Mental disciplines for healing, enduring pain, master escape artist, many forms of fighting.

Bruce was supposed to have a hatred for guns - not conceal one in public for revenge.

9.title: One of the best British films ever made!!!
9.content:
Though some may disagree, who prefer darker, edgier British cinema this is a piece of work that can show America that British films aren't all low budget and dull.

By the way, if at this point there is any dispute as to whether Batman Begins is a British film or not, the way I justify it is; 1) Practically all of the main cast are British (Christian Bale, Michael Caine, Liam Neeson, Cilian Murphy, Gary Oldman, Tom Wilkinson) the only real exceptions of course being Morgan Freeman and Katie Holmes. 2) The director is English 3) 2/3 of the movie was filmed either on location around Britian or in a London studio.

British!!!!

9.title: It's a new milestone in superhero movies and barely knew better things lay ahead.
9.content:
Batman certainly has always been the most famous and important character of DC Comics universe. Previously, the film portrayed the character with two distinct approaches with Tim Burton and Joel Schumacher. With the monumental failure of Batman & Robin, the damage done in the image of the Dark Knight was so great that other adaptations have been set aside for eight years. It was then that she was the revolutionary and brilliant Christopher Nolan, the director of the excellent Memento (2000) and Insomnia (2002), stunned the world with his vision. The Warner Bros. wanted to revive the story of the hero. After trying to contact some directors, Christopher Nolan himself presented his vision of the character. The British director has always been a fan of the character, but was not an expert on comic books. So even called a fan of the character to help him to write, David S. Goyer.

Goyer, Nolan and production designer Nathan Crowley began meeting then in Nolan's garage, where they began to develop the script and exchange ideas for large sequences. Crowley was shaping to Gotham City, the Batmobile and other elements into amazing models, working on the construction of Gotham. The city has never been more realistic, given that Burton has created a Gotham biggest concern with language abusing the dark and Schumacher had used the entire color palette in his films. The scenarios were built in huge studios and based in New York and Chicago mostly, but the director did not want it all done in a movie studio and get that goal.

9.title: Batman Back After Long Layoff
9.content: Christopher Nolan is one of filmdom's newer directors who never seems to let us down. His Batman Begins is the first Batman film in eight years, and what a dandy it is. The film is a much harder edged characterization of Batman and Gotham City than we've seen previously. Christian Bale is perfectly cast as a more realistic Batman than Michael Keaton, Val Kilmer, and especially George Clooney. This film has noir-like elements and the cinematography was Oscar-nominated. The soundtrack was grand but not intrusive like some movies of this type. The supporting roles were all mostly well cast, especially the villains. Katie Holmes, Cillian Murphy, and Tom Wilkenson actually help the film retain some of the comic book qualities associated with the character. Liam Neeson fits the current mold of a Hollywood nemesis with a mysterious past. While Micheal Caine and Gary Oldman disappear into their characters of Alfred and Gordon respectively, Morgan Freeman, as Luscious Fox, comes the closest to being a Hollywood distraction. However, Freeman is very enjoyable as always. Outside of the standard superhero moments and plot at the center of the film, we get to see how Batman came into being, how he came to be a superior fighter, and how he developed the many trademarks associated with him: Bat-cave, Bat-mobile, Bat outfit, and why the whole bat thing. Gone are the campy and over-the-top Batman elements from previous films. The film also marks a transition point from its comic realm with the lopping off of the Falcone character. The film stops short of exploring the public idolization of the character, but it does hint at it a couple times. The action of the plot resolution does echo too many other films though. Still, it's a superior and vastly entertaining action/comic book hero movie that delivers. Although like many other films, I think it definitely appears much too high on the IMDb's top 250 list. ***1/2 of 4 stars.

9.title: One of the best action films of the year, redefining just who Batman is.
9.content:
Most everybody enjoys a good action movie from time to time (or even all the time), and 'Batman Begins' is no exception. This film, directed by Christopher Nolan, almost redefines how we see the characters of both Batman and Bruce Wayne.

The film itself is set with a dark and intense look at each of the characters. First impressions are always the most important, and Christopher Nolan was quite aware of this fact from the moment he began looking at this script as can be seen from the final copy of this film.

From the beginning, it's obvious that Bruce Wayne isn't your typical multi-billionaire; being locked into a prison under his own free will to go day-to-day, fighting hordes of inmates for survival and the rush. We see that throughout the film (through flashbacks), Bruce had utter contempt for his family name after the passing of his parents, not caring for much else other than revenge against his parents murderer. Coldness towards life was a very jarring emotion displayed by the character we all know and love from the comic books and past movies. As the film continues, a definite change is taking place from within Wayne as he encounters 'Ducard,' a very skilled ninja who takes him in as an apprentice to teach him discipline and guidance, as well as mastering his fears. Once trained, he seems to be full of life once more, taking an active part in helping to better society, risking his life as our hero 'Batman.' Christian Bale has performed excellently within his role as Bruce Wayne and also as Batman. His performance as a cold-hearted young man is very striking and creates a lasting impression of his acting abilities. His movements seemed to flow in front of the camera, leaving the impression that he had been on screen all his life.

The supporting actors such as Liam Neeson (Henri Ducard), Kaitie Holmes (Rachel Dawes), Cillian Murphy (Dr. Jonathan Crane/Scarecrow), Michael Caine (Alfred), Morgan Freeman (Lucious Fox), and Gary Oldman (Jim Gordon), all performed fantastically on screen, portraying each character as if they all could support their own storyline and series, as every character should.

Liam Neeson provided the perfect villain as 'Ducard,' his presence on camera quick to strike both awe and illicit a shiver at the thought of the character. His portrayal of a man angered with society was flawless throughout the film, his previous film experience quite an asset.

Katie Holmes is a relative newcomer to the camera, but her acting as 'Rachel' may imply otherwise. She displayed a headstrong and assertive character, knowing exactly what she wanted and someone who would fight for it. Her romantic involvement with 'Bruce Wayne' was performed beautifully, not in any way harming the film at all.

Perhaps the darkest character of all within the film is portrayed by Cillian Murphy. 'Dr. Jonathan Crane' was a very sinister and dark character throughout the film, even as he played the 'innocent' psychiatrist, as opposed to his masked character 'Scarecrow.' Cillian was able to present the camera with such a dark 'aura,' that even being seen without having to speak any words, caused a slight chill to run up the spine of the viewer. Like Holmes, Cillian Murphey is still considered a newcomer to the screen, having been in lesser-known films in the past, but his work on this film is definitely worthy of note for his future career.

Michael Caine's supporting role as 'Alfred' was performed flawlessly as both a friend and father-figure to Bruce Wayne. His constant love and support is shown as Bruce's life follows from day to day, as well as his frustration with the young man. The acting job was well done, leaving us with a bit of a brand new look upon our favorite butler, offering bits of comedy, but still retaining the seriousness required for the character.

The storyline in and of itself is quite dark, offering us insight as to how 'Batman' was born into society and how Bruce was trained. The plot line has been done before many times; bad guy tries to destroy the city, good guy has to run and stop him...but the way Christopher Nolan presented us with his directing abilities, it displayed it within a new light, not the same, boring old stories we read and see everyday in entertainment. It left the film open to following sequels which (hopefully) will follow with the same stunning performances and sequences as this film presented.

The music fit the picture perfectly. Hans Zimmer delivered an astounding soundtrack of symphony that brought the action sequences to life and the serious, dramatic moments just the right touch to present us with a perfect atmosphere. The soundtrack was as audibly appealing as the movie is visually, helping to send each audience member to the edge of their seat as the music invaded every ear. The soundtrack is available through Warner Home Video, also through most popular and mainstream music stores.

All in all, 'Batman Begins' is the best movie within the Batman franchise, creating a fresh and new look at the 'Dark Knight' and characters we've all grown up knowing and seeing through previous shows and movies. This film redefines the 'Batman' film franchise, hopefully causing a certain 'revival' within fans and non-fans of the 'Batman' genre across the globe. It is a beautiful mixture of sound and visual effects, a stunning and exhilarating feast for the senses of anyone willing to pick up a copy. It's definitely worth the $5 new release rental fee, or the $18 purchase price-tag.

9.title: This is the definitive Batman movie.
9.content:
Wanna watch anything Batman? Start here. Batman Begins truly lives up to its title. It's the first, and probably only, Batman movie, to actually feel like a Batman movie.

All the installments prior had their focus set primarily on the villains. All the installments after have their focus set primarily on the drama. This one has its focus set on Batman.

That's what Chris Nolan set out to do since 2003, and it's what he has achieved completely. The entire movie is a testament to the very essence that is Batman. With its powerful Frank Miller source material to thank, Batman Begins is a much darker take on Gotham's Dark Knight.

Christian Bale's Batman voice in this movie is actually pretty good. It's not as hoarse and sluggishly stupid as the one in The Dark Knight and The Dark Knight Rises. His performance as Bruce Wayne, well, I gotta say, I can't imagine anyone else taking on the role. There may be many other actors who have made a better Batman, but Bale is definitely the only truly great Bruce Wayne.

Gary Oldman gives a nuanced and mostly subtle performance as Lieutenant Gordon in this one. Michael Caine has pretty much made the character of Alfred his own. It's really original, not to mention genuine. Liam Neeson is great in his role. Morgan Freeman was especially good in this movie.

Rutger Hauer, Cillian Murphy and Tom Wilkinson, all are really good in their roles. Katie Holmes is OK as Rachel, the assistant DA of Gotham.

The effects for Batman Begins are great, and have mostly aged really well. Some of the explosions may be a little too much, but the fear effects are really nice.

Overall, Batman Begins is an intense origin story of one of the greatest superheroes ever. It succeeds on all levels. While it's not my favorite of the trilogy, nor is is the best, it's still the definitive Batman movie. An excellent start to an above-excellent trilogy.

9.title: atman Begins: A Dark and Riveting Rebirth of the Caped Crusader
9.content:
Rating: 9/10 The Dark knight is a better movie but this is a better Batman movie.

Christopher Nolan's "Batman Begins" serves as a cinematic masterpiece that not only revitalizes the iconic superhero genre but also redefines the origin story of one of the most beloved comic book characters, Batman. With a perfect balance of gripping storytelling, stunning visuals, and exceptional performances, this film sets the stage for a new era in superhero cinema.

Christian Bale delivers a stellar performance as Bruce Wayne, bringing depth and humanity to the character. His journey from a disillusioned and vengeful young man to the formidable Dark Knight is portrayed with raw emotion and conviction. The film's exploration of Bruce Wayne's internal struggles and personal demons adds layers to the character, elevating him beyond the typical superhero archetype.

The supporting cast is equally impressive, with standout performances from Michael Caine as Alfred, Gary Oldman as Jim Gordon, and Liam Neeson as the enigmatic Henri Ducard. Each actor brings nuance to their roles, contributing to the film's overall sense of realism and gravitas.

Nolan's direction is masterful, and his decision to ground the story in a more realistic and gritty world sets "Batman Begins" apart from its superhero counterparts. The dark and atmospheric cinematography, coupled with Hans Zimmer's haunting score, creates an immersive experience that keeps audiences on the edge of their seats.

The film's narrative structure, expertly woven between present-day events and flashbacks, allows viewers to witness the evolution of Bruce Wayne into Batman. The exploration of fear as a powerful weapon and the philosophical themes of justice and morality add intellectual depth to the film, making it more than just a typical superhero action flick.

The action sequences are intense and well-choreographed, showcasing Batman's martial arts prowess and gadgetry. Nolan's commitment to practical effects and minimal use of CGI adds a tangible and authentic feel to the film's visual spectacle.

While "Batman Begins" serves as an origin story, it also lays the foundation for Nolan's celebrated "The Dark Knight" trilogy. The film's success in reimagining the Batman mythos and setting a new standard for superhero storytelling makes it a pivotal entry in the genre.

In conclusion, "Batman Begins" is a triumph on multiple fronts - from its character development and performances to its atmospheric cinematography and thought-provoking themes. Christopher Nolan's vision for the Caped Crusader is a resounding success, making "Batman Begins" a must-watch for both fans of the superhero genre and cinema enthusiasts alike. With a score of 9/10, this film stands as a testament to the enduring power of a well-crafted superhero narrative.

9.title: Great Beginning for Batman.
9.content:
After 8 years, the Batman franchise is revived with "Batman Begins." This is a great film where it depicts explicitly how Bruce Wayne came to become his alter ego, Batman. He (Christian Bale) goes to Asia and gets trained by a ninja cult leader. He returns to Gotham City in time to see it being overwhelmed by crime and corruption, which is when he found his calling. Unlike the previous Batman films of the late 1980s to 1990s, this film elaborates on important elements like Bruce's first encounter with bats, the discovery of the cave (Batcave) under his mansion and the creation of the Batmobile and Batsuit.

This film returns to its roots as a dark, somber and powerful film, which matches the mood and personality of Bruce Wayne/Batman, a departure from the campiness and cheesiness of the latter two Batman films of the 1990s. Each plot element was treated with care and had its own flavor. The part where Batman saves the little boy from Scarecrow (Cillian Murphy) depicts a true heroism; something that the boy can believe in-a hero and benefactor. In addition, the love/hate relationship between Bruce and Rachel Dawes (Katie Holmes) serves well as a sub-plot.

The special effects and stunts were outstanding, and each character performance was memorable. Michael Caine, Morgan Freeman and Gary Oldman were among the ones that gave great performances. It was clear that the budget for this film was generous, for there were good character development, great drama, mixed in with some humor. It is important to see how Bruce Wayne's relationship develops with Alfred, Luscious Fox and Commissioner Gordon, because it is clear that these people will be among the handful that will be true allies to Bruce/Batman.

Overall, a fantastic start to the Batman franchise, and hopefully, its sequels will be treated with equal care.

Grade A

9.title: A film that helped to redefine the superhero movie
9.content:
Having achieved critical acclaim for his three previous movies (all psychological thrillers) and commercial success for the last two of those, Christopher Nolan was hired to direct something rather different for his fourth film. With film studios suitably wowed by his talents, he was given the task of making the first Batman film for several years, and the result - Batman Begins - would catapult him to even greater success, lead to two sequels, and help to redefine the superhero movie.

Far darker than many people incorrectly remember the Tim Burton Batman films being, and with a more realistic approach than one might have expected at the time, Batman Begins focuses on the character of Bruce Wayne as he chooses to become a vigilante. With a screenplay written by Nolan and seasoned writer of comic book screen adaptations David S. Goyer, the first part of the film follows Wayne subjecting himself to brutal and rigorous training amongst criminals in Bhutan in his search for the means to fight injustice. Having travelled the world to understand the criminal mind, he receives a crucial part of his training from a man who turns out to be the film's principle villain. The second part of the film then sees him return to Gotham, don the Batman costume and fight supervillains, but in a way quite unlike any previous Batman film.

Basically, this is Batman dragged kicking and screaming into the real world and it works brilliantly. The fights are brutal, as the first scene with the adult Bruce Wayne demonstrates. Gotham is shot on location in three cities (New York, London and Chicago) and thus looks like a real place. We get two comic book Batman villains, but Ra's Al Ghul is written as - essentially - the leader of a terrorist cell, whilst the Scarecrow is a dodgy psychologist with a hint of drug dealer who wears a sackcloth hood. And it all looks incredible. Given a bigger budget than he had ever had to play with on first three films, Nolan doesn't waste a single penny, eschewing computer generated imagery where possible and favouring model work and a dizzying array of stunts instead. The soundtrack by Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard underscores the drama perfectly, the pair creating separate themes for Bruce Wayne and Batman.

The casting of method actor Christian Bale as Bruce Wayne is undoubtedly a key ingredient in the film's success, as he immerses himself in the lead role with utter conviction. Nolan assembles a strong cast including future regular collaborator Sir Michael Caine, who gives a remarkably gentle and dignified performance as Alfred, and Gary Oldman as James Gordon. Many of the main cast are British or Irish, with the most notable exceptions being Morgan Freeman, who plays Lucius Fox (and competes with Caine for most deadpan performance in the movie), and Katie Holmes as Rachel Dawes, a character created for the films. Cillian Murphy plays a wonderfully smarmy Scarecrow, whilst Liam Neeson - cast against type - makes an imposing and formidable Ra's al Ghul. Ken Watanbe, incidentally, plays the decoy Ra's al Ghul and sufficiently convincingly to make Neeson's true role a surprise. Quite why English actor Tom Wilkinson is cast as Carmine Falcone and required to adopt an American accent is unclear, but he gives a menacing performance nonetheless. He's a crucial ingredient of the background corruption that infests Gotham, in contrast to the more fantastical villainy of the Scarecrow and Ra's al Ghul.

The film is not all darkness - there are moments of warmth and humour, particularly between Bruce and Alfred and Bruce and Fox. It's also quite funny at times, such as when Bruce decides to live up to playboy expectations and buys a hotel, but these moments only serve to enhance the realistic air that Nolan is aiming for and in doing so thus help to balance out the more fantastical elements. Nolan had never directed what is essentially an action film before, but Batman Begins proved incredibly well how capable he was of doing so; the film is argued to have helped drive the comic book movie renaissance that followed, and it's easy to see why. One might describe Batman Begins as a masterpiece, were it not for the fact that it turned out to only be the first part in a trilogy - and the sequel that followed would prove to be even more impressive...

The movie is definitely quite long but more importantly, throughout the entire length of the movie, you wont really want to leave your seat. The acting talents of Christian Bale, Michael Caine have been fully utilized and the result is a worthy beginning movie for the great Batman series. Every aspect has been taken are of with panache, starting from how and why Bruce chose to be Batman to the most detailed developments of his Bat suit and car.Batman in this movie is no longer a smart superhero who fights villains, but a normal human being like you and me, a normal human being who has realized what he's capable of! All of this makes it not just a great beginning to the Batman series, but also one of the very best movies you're like to see in your lifetime!
